OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: I refer with profound sorrow to the passing away 
of Shri Parmeshwar Kumar Agarwalla, a former Member of this House on 
the 2nd August, 2005 at the age of 69 years. 
Born at Jharia in Dhanbad distri ct of Jharkhand in July, 1937, 
Shri Agarwalla had his education at DAV School, Jharia and School of 
Mining, Dhanbad. 
An industrialist by profession, Shri Agarwalla was associated with 
the coal industry for over four d ecades. He also had expertise in the steel 
and power sectors. He was President of the Industries and Commerce 
Association, Dhanbad, and was associat ed with various educational, social 
welfare and charitable institutions. He t ook keen interest in the upliftj of 
backward communities. 
Shri Agarwalla was a Member of Rajya Sabha for two consecutive 
terms from July, 1992 to July, 1998 and again from July, 1998 to July, 
2004 and represented States of Bihar and Jharkhand during the period. 
In the passing away of Shri Agarwa lla the country has lost a noted 
industrialist and a distinguished social worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Parmeshwar Kumar 
Agarwalla. 
I request Members to rise in thei r places and observe silence as a 
mark of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of 
the bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Now, Question Hour.

Statement 
(a) to (f) The Government sends representatives of Trade Unions to

*165. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: W ill the Minister of COMMUNICA- 
TIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that unscrupulous operators are

THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION

Statement 
(a) to (c) IT Enabled Services (ITES) or Business Process Outsourcing 
(BPO) in IT sector is a de-licensed activity. Such operations are governed 
by a contract between the parties. Government does not directly regulate 
such activities. However, as per information from NASSCOM, no such 
cases have been reported from their member companies.

holders to strengthen/safeguard Indian IT companies'

— Training and supporting Indian Law enforcement agencies to

— Establishment of a register of IT professionals by NASSCOM 
to ensure that only suitable staff is employed in the Industry.

Statement 
(a) and (b) The Government does not agree that the Indian Scientist 
is a case of pointless and indolent rese arch. On the other hand, considering 
the limited resources and facilities available for research, the Indian 
scientists have indeed performed well during the last five decades. The  
Green and the White Revolutions have converted India into a food surplus 
country. Our capabilities in the areas of space and nuclear research are 
well-known examples of what Indian science has achieved in the past. 
More recently, the Indian scientists and technologists have demonstrated 
their capabilities in several areas of emerging technologies such as the 
production of the first genetically engineered Hepatitis-B Vaccine, the 
indigenous development of small civilian aircrafts, ocean-based desalination 
plants for fresh drinking water, development of new drugs for diseases of 
importance to this country, such as tuberculosis, etc. These achievements 
indeed place India on a platform  of confidence as we enter the 
21st century. We foresee major developments through public-private 
partnerships resulting in increased a llocation of resources to scientific 
research and thus to increased contribution to the national economy. 
(c) Universities are the largest p ool of research manpower. The 
Government of India, on its part, has taken a number of steps to rejuvenate 
and promote scientific research in universities and other scientific institutes 
of excellence. The Plan Allocation of scientific departments has gone up 
from about Rs. 12000 crore in the Ninth Plan to about Rs. 25000 crore in 
the Tenth Plan. The Research Infrastruct ure programme of DST is a targeted 
programme to upgrade the laboratory infrastructrue in universities and other 
higher educational institutions. Several institutions, centres of excellence - 
and facilities in emerging and frontline areas have also been established; 
for example, in the areas of Brain Research, Marine Biotechnology, Stem 
Cell and Tissue Engineering, Soft Computing, Water Resources 
Development, Nanophosphors, Display Technology, Fuel Cell Technology, 
Ultrafast Processes, Protein Research, etc. 
The Government has also started some novel programmes to make 
our higher educational institutions professionally even more useful for 
developing technology. The DST programme of manpower development in 
collaboration with industry enhances the quality of technical education 
and makes it relevant for the industry through well-designed courses 
developed in close association with participating industries. A large network 
of S&T Entrepreneurship Parks and Technology Business Incubators has 
been established to synergize the technical expertise of engineering

institutions and the commercial spirit of entrepreneurs for technology 
development and commercialization. A large number of technology 
development projects are now being jointly undertaken by higher educational 
institutions and industries. All these are strong pointers towards 
improvement in indigenous capabilities for technology development.

used for any activities inimical to each othere's interests. The Indian side 
expressed its appreciation for actions taken by Bangladesh in the border 
areas and stressed the importance of  continued action consular access

161. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to" sell 100 years old former 
Indian Embassy Building in Bonn, Germany despite strong objection from 
the Indian Community in Germany: 
†Transliteration of Urdu Script. 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2005]

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) and (b) The Embassy of 
India 
shifted from Bonn to Berlin in October 1999 following a decision of the 
German Government to shift the capital to Berlin. A temporary office deal- 
ing with residual consular and administrative matters was maintained in 
Bonn up to June 2002, and was wound up with the opening of the new 
Consulate General of India in Munich. Consequently, the former Indian

the German State of North-Rhine West phalia, where Bonn is located, re- 
garding possible alternate use of the premises. However, since it was not 
found possible to put the building to an efficient use in a cost effective 
manner, the Government of India has decided to sell the property in the 
best interests of the Government. A number of other countries already 
sold their diplomatic properties that were located in Bonn. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) The advertisement for sale of the Bonn property ap peared in the 
local newspapers on April, 15 and 17,2005 inviting bids by May 17,2005.

deadline was extended to June 17,2005 following requests from prospec- 
tive buyers for more time. The sale of the property had been advertised for 
obtaining sealed competitive bids.

Coal and lignite reserves in the country 
1127. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state: 
(a)the estimated reserves of coal and lignite in the country at present; 
(b)the requirement of coal and lignite annually; 
(c) whether aiming for a gross domestic product growth of seven- 
eight per cent, Coal India Ltd. and Neyveli Lignite Corporation propose to 
increase their production; 
(d)if so, the details thereof; 
(e)whether Government are keen on investing in frontier technolo- 
gies such as exploration of coal bed methane and underground coal 
gasification; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) The es timated coal resources in the 
country are 247846.85 million tonnes as assessed by Geological Survey 
of India as on 1.1.2005. The estimated reserves of lignite in the country as 
on 1.4.2005 are 37154 million tonnes. 
(b) The all India coal demand in 2005- 2006 as finalized by the Plan- 
ning Commission is 445.65 million tonnes and the requirement of lignite 
for Neyveli Lignite Corporation's (NLC) operation is 20.4 million tonnes for 
the year 2005-06.  
(c) and (d) Coal India Limited (CIL) produced 323.63 million tonnes 
raw coal (provisional) in 2004-05. Du ring Mid-Term Appraisal the targets 
for CIL has been revised upward to 373.00 million tonnes, for the terminal 
year of X Plan (2006-07) as comp ared to earlier projection of 350.00 
million tonnes made by the Working Group on Coal & Lignite, working out 
to a cumulative aggregate growth rate  (CAGR) of 5.36% as against 4.59% 
projected earlier. 
NLC has also programmed to incr ease the lignite production from 
the projected production level of 20.40 million tonnes in 2005-06. With the 
sanctioning of expansion of Mine-ll from 10.5 million tonnes per annum to 
15 million tonnes per annum and sanctioning of a new mine of 2.1 million 
tonnes per annum at Barsingsar, NLC's lignite mining capacity is pro- 
jected to increase from the present level of 24 million tonnes per annum to 
30.6 million tonnes per annum by 2009-10. 
66 

[4 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) and (f) Yes, Sir. Details of activities for promotion of Coal Bed 
Methane (CBM) and Underground Coal  Gasification (UCG) are given as 
under.— 
In order to harness CBM potential in the country, Government formu- 
 lated a CBM policy in 1997. A total of 16 CBM blocks have been awarded 
so far (3 on nomination basis, 5 under CBM-I round and 8 under CBM-II 
round) for exploration and production of CBM. In addition, a demonstration 
 project named Coal Bed Methane Recovery & Commercial Utilization has 
been taken up in collaboration with United Nations Development 
Programme (UNDP) and Global Environment Facility (GEF). The project 
has beensanctioned by Government of India in September, 1999 and is under 
imple- mentation at Sudamdih and Moonidih mines at BCCL. 
CIL and ONGC have decided to take up project for establishing UCG 
technology. A draft MOU has already b een approved by Board of Directors 
of CIL. Initial work of data exchange needed for identification of trial site 
has already been taken up. 
NLC proposes to take up a UCG project in a suitable lignite block in 
Rajasthan under Ministry of Coal's S & T programme and Department of 
Science & Technology funding at a total cost of Rs. 1125 lakhs.

more than in the previous year; 
78 

[4 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the reasons for its poor performance during the last few years; 
(c) what steps are proposed to be initiated to improve its performance 
and revenue generations; 
(d) whether there is any plan to im prove its efficiency and better 
utilization of the existing large work force; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL 
AHMAD): (a) Rs. 1475 crore was the projected deficit of the department in 
Revised Estimates 2004-05; the actual deficit for the year 2004-05 is yet 
to be finalized. However, as per provisional results available, the deficit 
should be lower than that projected. 
(b)Department of Posts has not performed poorly during the last two 
years. There is a decline in deficit from 1999-2000 onwards except in the 
year 2003-04 when there was a margin al increase in the deficit. This 
marginal increase was due to paymen t of arrears of haulage charges to 
railways due to a revision of rates with  retrospective effect. The Department 
is also providing a host of services as part of its Universal Service 
Obligations at a subsidy as per the policy of the Government. 
(c) The Department has been continuously taking measures to improve 
its performance and revenue generation by introducing premium products 
like Speed Post, Express Parcel Post, Media Post, e-post etc. to cross 
subsidize its Universal Service Obligations. Computerization of Speed Post 
Centres, Free Pick up facility, Door to Door delivery, Internet Base Track & 
Trace, Credit facility, State Speed Post Centres, National Speed Post Centres 
etc. have been/are being provided to improve the quality of performance and 
revenue generation. A monthly review of expenditures as well as Revenue 
Receipts is being carried out at Secretary level. 
(d)and (e) To improve efficiency of the system and its capacity to 
generate revenues, the Department has initiated a number of measures 
under Plan to modernize it and induct technology into the various operations. 
Approximately 79% of the overall Tenth Plan outlay of Rs. 1350 crores has 
been earmarked for this purpose. Co mputerisation of post offices is a 
major initiative, which will increase the efficiency and producti-vity of the 
Department. Further Computerisation of Speed Post Centres and 
Registration Sorting Centres is unde r way to improve the quality of 
performance and revenue generation. The postal network is being

DR. KARAN SINGH:

(a) whether during Chinese Prime Minister's visit to India, both 
countries have taken a major step forward in agreeing a eleven point 'political 
parameters and guiding principles' to resolve their long standing boundary 
dispute between the two countries;

proactively addressing the issue as a 'strategic objectives'; 
(c) if so, to what extent this decision has helped in reaching the 
panel agreement on border between India and China; and

reached?

Indo-Bangladesh Foreign Secretary-level talks 
1160. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the issues discussed and the decisions taken at the Foreign 
Secretary level talks between India and Bangladesh held at Delhi in June 
last; and 
(b) the steps taken and proposed to be taken to implement them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) Foreign Secretary-level talks took 
place from 21-22 June, 2005. Issues  relating to security, peaceful 
management of the borders, cross border illegal movement of people, 
cooperation in water resources, economic  and trade cooperation, investment 
promotion, cooperation in science and technology and agriculture, defence 
exchanges and cultural relations were discussed. Both sides highlighted 
the importance they attach to bilateral relations and their sincere desire to 
further expand, deepen and strengthen their cooperation. 
Following are the decisions taken during the talks:— 
• The two sides reaffirmed their commitment not to allow their territory 
to be used for any activities inimical to each other's interests. 
• The two sides agreed to facilitate repair and development works 
along the India-Bangaladesh border. 
• The two sides decided to expedite the early conclusion of the Treaty 
on Mutual Cooperation for Preventing Illicit Trafficking in Narcotics 
and Psychotropic Substances, Bilateral Investment Protection and 
Promotion Agreement (BIPPA) and Cultural Exchange Programme. 
• The two sides agreed to strengthen measures to combat trafficking 
in women and children. 
• The two sides agreed to the early convening of the next round of 
Home Secretary level talks. 
• The two sides decided to resume meetings of the Joint Boundary 
Working Groups (JBWG) to consider boundary-related issues 
• The two sides agreed to address issues related to exchange of 
enclaves and territories in adverse possessions. 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2005] 
• The two sides agreed to the convening of the Joint Rivers 
Commission in Dhaka at a mutually convenient time. 
• The two sides agreed that the revised Trade Agreement be signed 
at an early date. 
• The two sides agreed that the bilateral Joint Working Group on 
Trade, para-tariff and non-tariff barriers and on customs matters 
should meet by August, 2005. 
• It was agreed to explore the possibility of commencing Dhaka- 
Guwahati, Dhaka-Shillong, Dhaka-Siliguri bus services. 
• The two sides agreed to carry fo rward discussions relating to the 
tri-nation gas pipeline. 
• The two sides agreed to increase cooperation in the fields of 
Agriculture and Science and Technology. 
(b) The Ministry of External Affairs has initiated action on the above 
decisions with the concerned Ministri es/departments and agencies in the 
Government of India.

Conversion of sea water into potable water 
1186. SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRIMATI N. P. DURGA: 
Will the Minister of OCEAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a)whether it is a fact that a new technology has been developed to 
convert sea water into potable water with a lesser cost; 
(b)if so, the details of the technology; 
(c) whether any experiments have been carried out to demonstrate 
the new technology; 
(d)if so, the details thereof; 
(e)whether it is also a fact that with  the new technology the cost of 
conversion of sea water into potable water comes to around 22 paise per 
litre; and 
(f) if so, whether it is viable? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. National 
Institute of Ocean Tech nology (NIOT), Chennai, an autonomous body of 
the Department, has developed a Low Temperature Thermal Desalination 
System (LTTD) technology for conversion  of sea water into potable water. 
The LTTD is a process by which fresh water is produced by flashing warm 
surface sea water under low vacuum c onditions and condensing the vapour 
using cold deep seawater. , 
(c) and (d) After successful experi ments in the laboratory NIOT 
demonstrated the LTTD Technology on an experimental basis on a barge 
mounted plant off Tuticorin , which successfully produc ed 10 lakhs litres in 
a 10-day period and the water quality is found to be excellent. In the 
meantime NIOT has set up a LTTD plant with a capacity of 1-lakh liter per 
day, at Kavaratti in Lakshadweep.  A 600m long pipe  was successfuly 
deployed for drawing the cold water. The heavy plant components were 
fabricated and installed. The plant was successfully commissioned in May 
2005. The water produced is of excellent quality. The plant is generating 
about one lakh litre per day. 
(e) and (f) At present, the cost of conversion of sea water into potable 
water works out to around 25 paise per litre at Kavaratti, Lakshadweep, of 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2005] 
which the running cost for power is about 6 paise per litre and the balance 
is for repayment of capital. However, the cost is expected to come down 
further once higher capacity desalination plant is commissioned and run 
over a long period.

NDC meeting 
1197. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the decisions arrived at with consensus during National 
Development Council Meeting held in Delhi on June 27th and 28th, 2005; 
(b) whether any machinery has been set up to ensure prompt and 
speedy implementation thereof; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The National Development Council 
met under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister on 27 th & 28 th June, 
2005 to consider the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Five Year Plan and 
took the following decisions: 
1. The NDC expressed broad agreemen t with the goals and policies 
suggested in the Mid-Term Appraisal which could act as a blue print for 
further action on development matters in the Tenth Plan and as the starting 
point for initiating work on the eleventh Five Year Plan. The Planning 
Commission was directed to examine a number of valuable suggestions 
made by Chief Ministers during the course of discussions which require a 
review of some of the policies, programmes and approaches. 
2. The NDC took note of the concerns expressed by the Chief 
Ministers about issues relating to Stat e finances, particularly the effects 
of the recommendations of the 12 th Finance Commission, the level of 
permissible market borrowings and interest costs on borrowings as also 
issues relating to mineral royalties and externally aided projects. It was 
decided to set up a Committee separately under the Finance Minister to 
examine relevant issues relating to the debt burden of States and debt 
relief with reference to their debt outstandings against the national Small 
Savings Fund (NSSF). 
3. Recognizing the fact that agriculture and irrigation have been a 
common theme in the interventions of the Chief Ministers, and that 
rejuvenating the agricultural credit system, providing some measure of 
relief to farmers, improving the quality of our extension work, attending to 
the specific needs and problems of dry lands and wastelands and enhancing 
investments in irrigation have emerged as common concerns, the NDC 
agreed to form a Sub-Committee for drawing up implementable action 
140 

[4 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
plans in agriculture and related issues. The NDC Sub-Committee is 
expected to submit its report within the next six months for inclusion in 
the Approach Paper to the Eleventh Five Year Plan. 
4. On the Employment Guarantee Act, the suggestions   that 
. payment of wages should be mostly in cash since there were problems in 
movement of foodgrains to backward areas and that being the self-targeting 
programme, the Employment Guarantee" should cover non-BPL families 
were noted by the NDC, and it was directed to consider them for inclusion 
in the final draft of the National Employment Guarantee Bill. 
5. To look into the need for providing adequate flexibility in the design 
of Centrally Sponsored Schemes, su ch as Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, the 
National Rural Heaith Mission and Bharat  Nirman etc., to take account of 
State level realities and priorities, as we ll as the feasibility of their transfer 
to States/UTs or amalgamation into four or five broad heads with the 
freedom to develop locally relevant programmes, the NDC directed the 
Planning Commission to consider setting up an Expert Group to develop 
concrete proposals for restructuring the CSS in consultation with the 
concerned Ministries/Departments. 
6. Recognizing that improvement in physical infrastructure has also 
emerged as a common priority and in creased private participation has 
now become a necessity to mobilize th e resources needed to achieve its 
expansion and upgradation, the NDC observed that successful promotion 
of private participation in infrastructure requires a well-designed framework 
of policies, in which investors have the assurance that standards of services 
will be maintained and concessions will be transparently awarded and 
directed the Central Government to work towards evolving such a framework, 
which could be adopted by the States. 
7. The Planning Commission was directed to begin work on the 
Approach to the Eleventh Five Year Plan with a view to submit it for National 
Development Council's approval by the end of December, 2005. 
 
(b) No Sir.

(SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) According to the Human Development Report 
2003, India is home to the largest number of hungry people (around 22% 
of India's population). However, as per the information from National Sample 
Survey Organization (NSSO), the percentage of households where all 
members did not get enough food everyday throughout the year was only 
3.8% in rural areas and 1.4% in urban areas for the year 1999-2000. 
(b) It has been the constant endeavour of the Government to strengthen 
various programmes to tackle the problem of poverty and food and nutritional 
security at the household level. This is sought to be achieved through the 
Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) under which foodgrains are 
provided to the poor at half the economic cost, and the Antyodaya Anna 
Yojana (AAY), under which 2.5 crore families are provided foodgrains at 
highly subsidized rates. In addition, there are food based schemes which 
also address nutritional security. These include the Sampoorna Grameen 
Rozgar Yojana (SGRY), National Food for Work Programme (NFFWP), 
Mid Day Meal scheme and provision of nutritional supplements to pre 
school children through the ICDS system.

Forecasts by IMD 
1208. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have recently issued a directive that no other 
agency than the Indian Meteorologi cal Department can make public the 
annual long range monsoon forecasts; 
(b) whether the predictions of the IMD since 1988 have had high 
failure rate (of nearly 65%), especia lly the gross failure of its forecast 
during the 2002 drought year; and 
(c) whether IMD's impossing of its authority on similar research 
institutions in the country, can be extended to such institutions abroad, 
whose monsoon forecast are easily accessible to Indian media over 
websites? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) The Government has not issued 
any directive that no other agency  than the IMD can make public the 
annual long range monsoon forecasts. Since such forecasts have policy 
implications, IMD not only consults other organizations while arriving at 
the forecast, but also take s the approval of the Mini stry before issuing the 
same. Research groups working in the area of monsoon forecasting are 
free to publish their forecast as research results. 
(b) The long Range Monsoo n forecasts of the India Meteorological 
Department (IMD) are made after consulting all the Research 
Organizations whose inputs are fully taken into account. During the 
last 17 years (1988-2004), IMD forecas ts were qualitatively correct in 
15 years ( i.e. 88%). The exception was during 2002 and 2004 both of 
which were drought years. The 2002 drought was due to exceptionally 
low rainfall during the month of July (49% of long term period average) 
caused by unexpected sudden warming of sea surface over equatorial 
central Pacific that star ted in the month of June. This exceptionally 
deficient rainfall of July 2002 was not predicted by any prediction group 
in India or abroad. 
(c) Monsoon forecasting being a research subject across the world, 
IMD encourages research on monsoo n forecasting by other scientists 
outside IMD also.

1218. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, 
ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that two sh ips collided at Visakhapatnam 
Port, recently; 
(b) to what extent has lax piloting and port management been the 
cause of such accidents; 
(c) the number of such accidents that have taken place in the last 
two years at Visakhapatnam; 
(d) whether any enquiry has been do ne by a competent authority on 
this accident; and 
158 

[4 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) the steps that would be taken to  ensure that there are no such 
accidents in future? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPI NG, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The M.V. UTTAR 
KASI while shifting from outer harbour to  inner harbour, collided with M.V. 
CHIN SHWE HAW berthed at return end of West Quay 1. The accident 
occurred because the M.V. UTTAR KASI ship engine staff did not carry 
out astern movement as required an d instead carried out ahead movement 
the Inner Turning Basin of the harbour and the ship's Master, the ship's 
Duty officer and the port's pilot could not ascertain the same as the ship's 
RPM indicator in the wheel house was not working. The incident was not 
caused due to lax piloting or negligence of the port management. 
(c) No other incident of collision have occurred during the last two 
years. 
(d) Yes, Sir. An inquiry on the subject has been conducted by the 
Harbour Master of the Port. 
(e) Ports follow precautionary measures  necessary for safe movement 
of ships in the harbour area. The sh ips are moved by experienced pilots 
with assistance of tugs. In those cas es where maneuvering appears risky, 
additional tugs/additional pilots are used for safe movement and vessels 
are moved only during daylight hours. The safety measures have now 
been further enhanced by the port authorities. The Master of the vessel 
will be required to ensure that the indication for engine RPM on the 
wheelhouse of a ship should be working. The port pilots have been instructed 
to suitably brief the Masters of the ships soon after boarding and before 
undertaking the pilotage operation.

Monopolies of management in sports 
1263. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that monopolies of management have come to 
stay and dominate ail games and sports in the country; 
(b) in what manner Government are trying to change the scenario 
presently prevailing in the country; 
(c) whether any term limits would be imposed on any individual or 
group who continue to dominate the same game or sports from any State 
for decades together; 
(d) whether opinion has been sought on how to combat this stagnation 
in sports management all across the country; and 
(e) the steps proposed to open up sports management and 
administration in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) to (e) Sports activities are managed by 
the concerned National Sports Federa tions (NSFs) which are registered 
under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 under different State 
Governments and are autonomous in their functioning. The Government of 
India does not interfere in their day-to-day functioning, including their 
management. The election of office bearers of these federations are 
governed by the provisions of their Memorandum of Associations (MoA). 
The Guidelines for Assistance to National Sports Federations have 
provisions restricting tenure of office bearers of NSFs to two tenures of 4 
years each. 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2005] 
'Sports' figures in the 'State List' of the Constitution of India and the 
Central Government has no mandate to legislate on any matter concerning 
sports. However, the overall issue of sports management and role of 
Government of India was discussed with the Sports Ministers and 
Secretaries of the State Governme nts who attended the last Annual 
Conference. The specific issue of tenu re of office bearers of NSFs had 
also been discussed with IOA & NSFs from time to time in the past. 
Accordingly, it was decided to keep the provisions concerning tenure in 
abeyance, for the present.

two States. As reflected in the Statement, we are on a footing of quality 
not of tutelage. And, whatever little  I understand about international 
diplomacy, which is very little, it is that when Heads of State of two different 
countries sign a Joint Statement, they do not set out areas of their 
disagreement. Hence, you will find only one sentence on international 
terrorism which reads, "The conclusion of the UN Convention on 
International Terrorism proposed by India at an early date was deemed to 
be a priority of both countries". To me, this sentence is pregnant with the 
affirmation that each of us has main tained our respec tive positions on 
global terrorism. Lastly, Sir, one sentence in the Joint Statement is the 
reason why I sought for few minutes in this discussion session and it 
reads, "The President reiterated his vi ew that international institutions are 
going to have to adapt to reflect India's central and growing role." Obviously, 
President Bush meant the United Nations. My point, Sir, is, if international 
institutions are to adapt to reflect India's growing role, India must respond. 
But, to play an increasing role on the world stage, it is necessary for India 
to be UN Convention compliant. We should satisfy the conventions that 
we have already signed. We do not have any Constitutional impediments 
of parliamentary approval to conventions which are signed to be ratified. 
And, I particularly refer, Sir, to the Torture Convention. I was fortunate 
enough and privileged enough to join  a parliamentary delegation a few 
weeks ago to Strasbourg. Several Me mbers of the Euro pean Parliament 
asked us quite pointedly, to which I had very little to say, "You have signed 
the Torture Covention, why haven't yo u ratified it?" Because we do not 
have a constitutional impediment that our Parliament has to ratify, it is the 
Executive that ratifies it. So, if you signed a convention, you should ratify
  
it. This will certainly imporve our image on the world stage, especially 
when we have nothing to hide in the matter of this Torture Convention. That 
is all I wish to say, Sir. Thank you.

two countries, there are bound to be certain areas with which one country 
may not agree, and certain areas with which the other country may not

What i wish, therefore, to bring before the House today is not the points on 
which we feel happy or on which we feel unhappy. This has been done very 
well by previous speakers. But what I wish to deal with is that having 
signed this agreement, there are certain  areas where we have to be a little 
careful. I would say a lot to be careful. We have to be really vigilant. I want 
to bring out the past experience of our country with the Unites States, in 
particular about the Tarapore Project and supply of Nuclear Fuel. 
From that experience, we should learn this great lesson. And that is 
this. Okay, we go with this, but we should remain very, very careful. The 
experiences of the past convince us that if we are not careful, we can be 
tripped into one bad situation, and from that into a worse situation. I will 
just mention our experience. 
In 1963, we had signed a solemn agreement with the United States 
for supplying nuclear fuel for Tarapore for 30 years. It was to go on till 
2003. After Pokhran I, the U.S. star ted twisting us, breaking our bones, 
putting us in the dark house, putting us in a corner, in practically 20-25 
major areas of concerns to us. One of them was passing a legislation in 
the U.S. Congress regarding stopping su pply of nuclear fuel to India. We 
got terribly frightened at this prospect of having to close down the Tarapore 
Plant. The then Prime Minister, Mrs. Indira Gandhi, was going to visit the 
United States in 1982 somewhere near the end of July and beginning of 
August. The mandate given to us by her was that before we leave, we shall 
try to sort out all issues, particularly Tarapore issue. 
Tortuous negotiations were held with the American Ambassador and 
his advisor by people like me, the Fo reign Secretary, Chairman of the 
Atomic Energy Commission and the Cabine t Secretary. They  always turned 
back to us with this argument —"The President wants to give you the 
Tarapore fuel without interruption, but we have to be very careful about the 
Congress' attitude. And unless we take the Congress also with us, there 
will be trouble. Therefore,  you give us something more in return." We told 
them that it was an agreement signed and valid till 2003, and we could not 
be asked to make any concession. But they did not agree to it. Finally 
after a lot of arguments, we reached a settlement at official level saying 
that a third country will take this obligation. That third country was France, 
which had no difficulty on the point of view of a legislation by parliament. 
So, we thought it was an excellent arrangement

[4 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
As far as our nuclear programme is concerned, our scientists have 
done us proud by having mastered the complete fuel cycle. From 
Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors to Fast Breeders to Next Generation 
Reactors based on thorium, we will give them all possible facilities to 
realize this vast latent potential re presented by the Indian science and 
technology in the US. So, there should be no doubt in anybody's mind 
that the nuclear programme, that our research effort, will suffer. There 
should be no doubt that our strategic asset programme will not remain 
exclusively in our own hand and, at th e same time, we have the satisfaction 
that if what the President has promis ed me is really implemented by the 
Congress, we would have full equal status with regard to international 
trade in civilian nuclear facilities. 
I think if that comes about, it will open up a few possibilities of the 
development of India's nuclear energy system. We have today because of 
a small nuclear energy sector, only sm all firms, high technology firms, in 
which we can take great pride. I take pride in the activities of the Bharat 
Heavy Electricals Ltd. I take pride in the way Larsen and Tubro has 
managed the most modern technologies, and also Walchand Hirachand. 
But these are only small islands. If in  the next 20-30 years our nuclear 
power programme increases and we have the ambition to aim at 30,000 to 
40,000 megawatts of nuclear capacity in the next 20 years, I have a vision 
that this will bring about a new burst of creativity, a second industrial 
revolution based on high technology where we will find many more new 
firms mastering the complicated new technologies now operating on the 
frointiers of scientific knowledge and technology. Now Dr. PC. Alexander 
said, "there are risks. US may not live up to what they promise." In life 
nothing is very certain, I think we have all to work on the assumption that 
things ex post may not turn out to be what they appear to be in sight. We 
must, therefore, take precautions. But not take risks would also be an act 
of lethargy. What is necessary is that we, as a nation, should take 
calculated risks. I submit to this august House that what we have done 
during our visit is, if there are risks,  those are calculated risks; they are 
worth taking. While I am on subject, I would like to conclude by paying 
tribute to the team of officials wh o worked hard. The Chairman of the 
Atomic Energy Commission, Dr. Kakodkar; the National Security Advisor, 
Mr. Narayanan; the Foreign Secretary, Mr. Shyam Saran; our Ambassador 
in Washington, Mr. Ronen Sen, all working actively under the guidance of 
my colleague, Shri Natwar Singh. I th ink they deserve our appreciation for 
what they have done.
